description: PasswordsCon talks from BSides Las Vegas 2025.

talks.title: Taking down the power grid!
talks.teaser: Follows a red team engagement that clones access cards and reaches a server room guarding a national power grid.
talks.summary:
This red team war story follows an engagement against a large power company, where anything was allowed except harming people or property. The goal was to reach a shielded server room in a basement and leave a dummy device simulating a bomb that could disable the grid's control systems. The team started with online and physical reconnaissance, then phished for domain credentials.

Next, the team found the cards used an older MIFARE Classic format and used a Flipper Zero near a reader to pull the data needed to recover keys. Lacking a commercial skimmer, they improvised one from a Raspberry Pi, a Proxmark, a power bank and a 4G modem, hidden in an electrical enclosure taped beneath a reader. A telescope from a rented van captured PIN entries, and a few cards were read. Cloned cards opened the outer door but not the server room. During office hours the team waited in a restroom, then reached the internal network from an office socket after 802.1x blocked other ports. The access control server accepted RDP with a default-style administrator login, which let them change their card's access rights and enter the room.

The team left the dummy device, removed their card permissions and walked out. The client was surprised the room was reachable and later changed its access control technology, while staff were told to shield PIN entry. Recommendations included stronger card technology such as DESFire, no default passwords, and limiting remote desktop access to users who need it. The speaker noted the cameras had been turned off.

talks.title: Phish-Back: How to turn the problem into a solution
talks.teaser: Shows how a decoy login portal can expose attackers reusing stolen credentials so defenders can reset them early.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the problem of stolen credentials, which remain a leading initial access route despite security training, phishing simulations, dark web monitoring and MFA. The speaker, a former SOC manager, describes an incident in which a handful of employees gave up valid logins to a phishing email, and attackers then reached a newly opened subsidiary that had not enabled MFA, all within about a day.

The proposed countermeasure, called Phish-Back, places a convincing decoy login portal among the real VPN gateways so that attackers who test stolen credentials against it reveal themselves early. The main difficulties are making the decoy pass fingerprinting by internet scanners, which compare response hashes, headers and page structure, and reproducing the exotic endpoints, languages and HTTP methods that a real product exposes. The speaker also stresses choosing a domain name that blends into the target's external footprint, and filtering the heavy background noise of internet traffic with checks such as password policy, name patterns, leaked-password lookups and validation against the directory before any account is reset.

Across roughly 50 portals deployed at about 20 large organisations over a year and a half, the speaker reports 2.3 billion login attempts and 257 valid credentials that had no dark web exposure. The takeaway is that the approach only works with careful execution and strict filtering, and that dark web monitoring alone is far from exhaustive.

talks.title: What to Tell Your Developers About NHI Secrets Security and Governance
talks.teaser: Explains how non-human identities and hardcoded secrets create risk, and how to raise the issue with developers.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses non-human identities (NHIs), meaning the service accounts, bots and running workloads that authenticate to other systems using secrets. The speaker argues that these identities now far outnumber human ones, often by around a hundred to one, and that fast, AI-assisted development is multiplying them. Credential misuse is a leading route into breaches, so the speaker frames the problem as a governance gap rather than only a developer mistake.

The middle of the talk walks through the OWASP top ten risks for NHIs, grouped into three buckets for conversations with developers. Themes include assigning a clear owner to each identity, planning offboarding and decommissioning, scoping permissions narrowly instead of granting broad access, avoiding reuse of one identity across environments, and asking whether a human should ever use a given identity. The speaker cites his company's research on public GitHub commits, which found millions of hardcoded secrets added in 2024 and many still valid when rechecked months later.

For practitioners, the closing advice is to raise awareness with the people who write the code first, then set policies, then deploy tools. Technical steps include moving secrets into a secret manager and referencing paths instead of values, rotating credentials automatically, adopting short-lived workload identities, and using Git hooks and pull request checks to block or replace hardcoded secrets. Tooling comes last, and training developers to follow the process is stressed throughout.

talks.title: Cracking Hidden Identities: Understanding the Threat Surface of Hidden Identities and Protecting them Against Password Exposure
talks.teaser: Examines unmanaged SaaS accounts outside corporate identity providers and how weak, reused passwords expose organizations.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that many accounts employees use fall outside what an organization's identity provider and password policies can see. The speaker, whose company runs a browser extension that observes real employee activity, defines hidden identities as personal accounts used for work, non-SSO corporate logins, temporary and third-party accounts, and chained identities. Using aggregated telemetry, the talk reports that over a 90-day window most software-as-a-service use was non-corporate, and that about half of corporate accounts sat outside single sign-on.

The middle section turns to password quality and exposure. Using a common strength-estimation library, the speaker reports that passwords used for personal activity are no stronger than those used at work, and that some stay unchanged for years. A small group, around two percent of users, combines heavy shadow SaaS use, weak passwords and frequent appearances in breaches. Reused credentials and personal webmail takeovers are presented as a route into business systems, illustrated by a publicly reported incident in which a contractor's personal email led to corporate access.

For practitioners, the advice centres on visibility first, then enforcement. Restrict non-work SaaS, enforce SSO wherever possible, and for non-SSO accounts validate that passwords rotate, sessions and cookies are flushed, and credentials are strong, ideally through a corporate password manager. Focus controls on the small high-risk group, and recognise that hostname-based network tools miss how users actually log in. The Q&A covered user buy-in, personal logins on sensitive systems, and balancing data security against access security.

talks.title: Extending Password (in)Security to the Browser
talks.teaser: Explains how malicious browser extensions access cookies and passwords, and what defenders can do about it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by framing the problem: organizations now authenticate users across many outside applications, and the session cookie that follows a login sits in the browser, where anything running there, including extensions, can read it. Extensions run whenever the browser is open, stay largely invisible to endpoint tools, and are tracked only by their ID, so an extension approved once can later be swapped for malicious code and keep its approval.

Eshed walks through the extension permissions that matter for credential theft, including cookie access, scripting and page content visibility, and argues that many store extensions request far more than they need. He describes how attackers obtain extensions through compromised developer accounts, purchase, or building their own, and presents a case where a cookie-stealing extension aimed at Microsoft Entra stopped working until the login added a factor kept in the browser cache, which the extension could also read.

On defense, the options reviewed were allow lists, block lists, banning extensions outright, and risk-based management that inventories extensions and versions across browsers and enforces policy through device management. Eshed points out the practical gaps: browsers differ in enterprise visibility, extensions change constantly, and enforcement is hard to automate. He closes by arguing that attackers will keep shifting toward the browser as other routes become harder.

talks.title: The Rise of Synthetic Passwords in Botnet & Attack Operations
talks.teaser: Explains how botnets generate high-entropy synthetic passwords to flood logins and evade breach-based detection.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces synthetic passwords as an emerging attacker tactic: credentials that are algorithmically generated, have never appeared in a leak, and are built at scale with scripts or AI to look human-like or to carry high entropy. The speaker argues that the goal is often not to get into accounts but to flood security operations with noise and mask credential stuffing, exploiting the assumption that a clean breach-database lookup means low risk.

The speaker showed a simple script that combines names, numbers and special characters to produce unique passwords that look realistic. In a comparison, most passwords taken from recent stealer logs appeared in a breach corpus, while none of the synthetic passwords did. The speaker explained how this weakens breach correlation, makes honeyword traps harder to trigger, and removes behavioural signals such as a single source or a repeated password pattern. Audience questions clarified that the approach works as a mix of brute forcing existing accounts and overwhelming the login service.

For defenders, the speaker recommended not relying on breach correlation alone. Suggested measures included entropy scoring, login pattern anomaly checks, session fingerprinting, and watching for failures that look too clean or sudden surges of highly varied inputs. The talk also proposed shifting detection from identity toward user intent and flagging non-human session patterns. The main takeaway is that a password missing from breach databases should not be treated as safe.

talks.title: Lessons from Black Swan Events and Building Anti-Fragile Cybersecurity Systems
talks.teaser: Argues that defenders should treat breaches as lessons, using anecdotes on shadow IT, default credentials and incident planning.
talks.summary:
Dave Lewis opens by framing security breaches as black swan events, drawing on Nassim Taleb's idea of rare, high-impact shocks that look obvious in hindsight. He points to recurring failures such as default device credentials behind large botnets, exposed cloud storage, and stale privileged accounts, arguing that many incidents could have been prevented with basic hygiene. He also notes that passwords are only one control, and that MFA, passkeys and extended access management reduce risk without eliminating it.

The middle of the talk covers organizational problems: shadow IT, unused incident response plans, forgotten services with no owner, and a copied policy that had been written for a swimming certification. Lewis describes ransomware trends from 2017 to 2023, including the shift toward smaller suppliers that connect to larger firms, and stresses non-blaming, open communication across finance, HR and other business units.

He closes by urging resilience and anti-fragility: systems that can absorb a hit and improve afterwards, practiced incident response, a dissenting voice on every review team, and realistic expectations about cyber insurance, which does not restore an organization on its own. He also flags caution around AI adoption. Practitioners should take away the need to plan for disruption rather than assume it will not happen.

talks.title: The HMAC Trap: Security or Illusion?
talks.teaser: Shows how HMAC misuse, weak keys, replay gaps and timing leaks can break authentication in systems that look secure.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how HMAC, a keyed hash used to confirm that a message is authentic and unchanged, gets misused in authentication. The speaker built a small Python client and server lab, first with MD5 and then SHA-256, and showed that a captured message and tag can be cracked offline when the key is weak. Intercepting traffic through a proxy showed that tampered messages and tags were rejected, yet recovering the key let forged messages pass.

Further demos covered a dictionary attack against an admin account's key, replay of messages when timestamps were missing or ignored, and a timing side channel created by a non-constant-time tag comparison. A logic flaw where the server accepted any tag was also shown, along with JSON Web Tokens that accepted the none algorithm or used a guessable signing secret. Each case was presented as a simple proof of concept.

The practical guidance centred on key management: long random keys rather than passwords, rotation and revocation, never hardcoding keys, least-privilege access, timestamps and nonces to block replay, constant-time comparison functions, and rejecting the none algorithm in tokens. The closing point was that HMAC itself is not broken but is often misused and mismanaged. Audience questions covered whether timing attacks are practical over a network, whether password-derived keys are acceptable, and the effect of quantum computing, and the speaker left the network timing question open.

talks.title: Password Expiry is Dead: Real-World Metrics on What Rotation Actually Achieves
talks.teaser: Shows cracked-password data from real organizations that undercuts forced password rotation and suggests risk-based alternatives.
talks.summary:
The talk questions the long-standing practice of forcing users to change their passwords on a fixed schedule. The speaker traces this guidance to roughly 2010 to 2012 and argues that forced expiry pushed users toward predictable patterns, such as appending or incrementing numbers, instead of stronger passwords.

The core of the talk is cracking data from four anonymised organisations, with rotation intervals ranging from 30 days to more than 120 days. In the shortest-interval environments, a large share of passwords fell to simple incremental rules, with overall crack rates between roughly 70% and 89%. Longer intervals reduced those patterns, but the speaker stressed that they did not make passwords uncrackable. He also covered side effects such as more help desk tickets and users writing passwords down.

For alternatives, the speaker suggested time-to-crack scoring of the domain, resets triggered by credential-leak events rather than the calendar, entropy tracking per user, and MFA with secure fallbacks. Hashcat features for auditing were also mentioned. The takeaway is that rotation alone is not an effective control, and it should be replaced by strong passwords combined with risk-driven response.

talks.title: I'm A Machine, And You Should Trust Me: The Future Of Non-Human Identity
talks.teaser: Argues that hardcoded, long-lived credentials make non-human identities a major breach risk and outlines practical fixes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a quick audience poll contrasting a suspicious phone call with an unexpected offer, to show that people apply gut checks that software does not. Non-human identities such as API keys, service accounts and workloads now outnumber people by wide margins, and the speaker argues that a valid bearer token gets access no matter who presents it. Credentials are often hardcoded, over-scoped and rarely rotated, so a single leaked key lets an attacker act as a machine without exploiting anything.

Using public secret-scanning figures and a practitioner survey, the speaker shows that many leaked secrets stay valid long after discovery. He frames the problem as one of ownership, asking who controls each credential and what its lifecycle and sunset policy is. For the long term, he points to federated workload identity, including SPIFFE and SPIRE and the IETF's emerging workload identity drafts, along with short-lived tokens such as Kubernetes service account tokens for image pulls. For the short term, he proposes finding every secret, moving it into a secret manager, scanning continuously, adding developer tooling such as git hooks, and automating rotation.

The closing message is to build a repeating cycle: raise awareness, assign ownership and write policy, then pick tools and train people. He also urges attendees to look after their own wellbeing while doing this work.

talks.title: Password Cracking in AD: The Fun Part of Compliance
talks.teaser: Shows how cracking your own Active Directory password hashes can turn compliance rules into a measurable control.
talks.summary:
The talk follows three fictional organizations, each with a different approach to password compliance, to show how the same policy rules hold up against an attacker. It opens with a common scenario: an internet-facing login is brute forced and password sprayed within hours of going online. One company is protected by multi-factor authentication and raises alerts, while the other is breached and its credential store is dumped.

The middle section compares PCI DSS, GDPR and NIST SP 800-63B guidance on password length, rotation and complexity. A cracking time table is used to show why longer passphrases without forced rotation can outlast short complex passwords. The speaker then demonstrates a self-audit workflow: a low-privilege service account replicates directory data, hashes are cracked on a schedule using hashcat with rules and PRINCE mode, and accounts with weak passwords are forced to change. Duplicate hashes across different accounts are flagged as either guessable passwords or a broken provisioning process. The same approach is shown for Entra ID using AADInternals, and cracked words are added to banned-password lists.

The closing point is that following standards blindly does not improve security, while applying them intelligently with user training and regular self-testing can. Practical advice includes storing long random passwords in a manager, using memorable long passphrases where typing is unavoidable, and rolling out policy changes in waves rather than all at once.

talks.title: Hazard Analysis of Military AI Systems Using STPA-Sec: A Systems-Theoretic Approach to Secure and Assured Autonomy
talks.teaser: Shows how threat intelligence sources overlap, lag and conflict, and what that means for defenders who rely on them.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why cyber threat intelligence often fails to help defenders, drawing on several years of indicator data from commercial providers, government and consortium sources, and open-source publishers. The speaker describes how many commercial producers are closed to outside customers, how feed volume and indicator counts grew between 2023 and 2025, and how little overlap exists between providers. Overlap is typically in the low single digits, and for newly emerging threats it can be far lower.

The middle section covers ambiguity and timing. Roughly one in six cases showed conflicting context about the same threat, and providers tend to focus on different parts of the attack lifecycle, so a single source can leave gaps. Analysis of vulnerabilities published in 2023 and 2024 found that many indicators were already in circulation before public disclosure, with attacker infrastructure appearing to shift in the days just before and after it. Case studies on a ransomware-as-a-service family and several infostealers showed how quickly coverage built up after publication.

The closing argument is that discarding older indicators without context can open blind spots, and that defenders should evaluate coverage across sources rather than relying on one or two feeds. The speaker put the odds of threat intelligence stopping a given attack at around five percent, and answered audience questions on predictive signals such as scanning activity seen ahead of disclosure.

talks.title: Machine Identity & Attack Path: The Danger of Misconfigurations
talks.teaser: Shows how one overly broad cloud permission can let an attacker escalate privileges across an entire organization.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining machine identities, such as service accounts, tokens and secrets used by applications, containers and pipelines, and contrasts them with human accounts. The speaker argues that a high-value target is not only an executive but anyone whose identity carries broad permissions. A Brazilian financial fraud case illustrates the point: a junior developer with excessive rights and no just-in-time access became the facilitator of the attack.

The middle section walks through AWS identity and access management, covering policy statements, effects, actions and resources, and why wildcard resources are risky. A live demonstration shows how read-only credentials can enumerate users and policies, and how a single permission to create policy versions lets an attacker grant themselves wider access, eventually at the organization level. Attack paths are presented as graphs, where a chokepoint is a single fix that cuts many routes to a high-value identity.

To close, the speaker recommends open-source mapping tools such as Cartography, AWSPX and SecBridge, which need only read-only access to build identity graphs, and mentions a free community edition of a commercial graph platform. Audience questions covered using access logs to strip unused permissions, and whether AI agents that run around the clock weaken just-in-time controls. The suggested answer was behaviour analytics. The main takeaway is to apply least privilege and review every permission.

talks.title: Cracking 936 Million Passwords
talks.teaser: Walks through cracking hundreds of millions of leaked NTLM password hashes using CPU rigs, custom rules and curated wordlists.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a public breach corpus of about 936 million NT LAN Manager password hashes and asks what it takes to recover plaintexts at that scale. The speaker explains why the fast, unsalted NTLM scheme is so easy to attack, and why slower, salted algorithms such as bcrypt make the same effort far more expensive. Hardware comparisons follow, with a high-RAM CPU machine outperforming a consumer GPU for this workload because of memory demands and tool behaviour.

The middle section covers method. Brute force over longer character sets becomes impractical quickly, and rainbow tables proved too slow for this volume. Dictionary attacks combined with mangling rules, mainly from John the Ripper plus a custom rule that inserts control characters, recovered most of the passwords. Recovered plaintexts were then reused as a new wordlist, and the speaker shared statistics on password length, character classes and unusual control characters that show how people construct passwords.

The closing advice is practical. Stored passwords should use slow, salted hashing, accounts that matter should have two-factor authentication, and people should rely on a password manager to generate long random passwords. The speaker also suggested that machine learning could eventually help produce better mangling rules.

talks.title: Reversing F5 Service Password Encryption
talks.teaser: Shows how F5 load balancers protect stored service account passwords and how those values can be recovered after a compromise.
talks.summary:
F5 load balancers are usually deployed as active and standby pairs that exchange configurations, including encrypted service account passwords such as LDAP bind credentials. This talk examined how those values are protected. Each stored password uses a dollar-M prefixed format, and its encryption depends on a master key that is itself wrapped by a unit key. The unit key sits in EPROM on physical hardware and on the filesystem for virtual appliances.

The speaker pointed out that an uppercase K option on the key management command is barely documented, yet it exposes a base64 key when used. With that key and the encrypted string, decryption is simple: strip the prefix, base64 decode the value, and run AES-128 in ECB mode. A live demo used a Python script to recover a password from a master key taken from a device, and the unit key could be used to derive the master key as well. In the Q&A, the speaker said FIPS-mode systems had not been tested, but expected the same synchronization dependency to make the approach workable there.

The main takeaway is that if an F5 is compromised, even encrypted service credentials should be treated as exposed, because everything needed to decrypt them is on the box. Responders handling an F5 incident should rotate the service account passwords stored on it.
